s4p1.title: Part 1 · MOS Capacitor and MOSFET Structure
s4p1.intro: A Field-Effect Transistor (FET) controls the current between two of its terminals with the electric field created by a voltage applied to a third terminal. The current flows through a channel, and the gate voltage determines how conductive this channel is. This chapter covers two types: the MOSFET (Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor FET) and the JFET (Junction FET).
s4p1.vlsi: The MOSFET is the primary component of high-density VLSI chips such as memories and microprocessors. A modern processor contains billions of MOSFETs, so the equations in this chapter underlie nearly every electronic device in use today.
s4p1.cap: To understand the MOSFET, start with its core, the MOS capacitor. Think of it as a parallel-plate capacitor:
s4p1.li1: First electrode, the Gate: made of a low-resistivity material (highly doped polycrystalline silicon, aluminum or tungsten).
s4p1.li2: Second electrode, the Substrate (Body): an n-type or p-type semiconductor.
s4p1.li3: Dielectric between them: silicon dioxide (SiO2), a stable, high-quality insulator between gate and substrate. As a result, no DC current flows into the gate.
s4p1.f1: C<sub>ox</sub>'' = ε<sub>ox</sub> / T<sub>ox</sub>    (F/cm<sup>2</sup>)     ε<sub>ox</sub> = 3.9ε<sub>0</sub> , ε<sub>0</sub> = 8.854×10<sup>-14</sup> F/cm
s4p1.cox: Cox'' is the oxide capacitance per unit area and Tox is the oxide thickness. A thinner oxide gives a larger capacitance (the plates are closer) and stronger gate control over the channel.
s4p1.ex1: Example: For Tox = 50 nm, Cox'' = 3.9·8.854×10-14 / (50×10-7 cm) = 6.91×10-8 F/cm2 = 69.1 nF/cm2. Since capacitance is inversely proportional to thickness, Tox = 20 nm gives 173 nF/cm2, 10 nm gives 346 nF/cm2 and 5 nm gives 691 nF/cm2.
s4p1.h2: Three conditions on a p-type substrate
s4p1.bias: The gate voltage VG determines what happens at the silicon surface just under the oxide. The critical voltage here is the threshold voltage VTN.
s4p1.li4: Accumulation (VG < 0): The negative gate attracts the majority carriers of the p-type substrate, the holes, to the region under the oxide. Holes accumulate at the surface.
s4p1.li5: Depletion (0 < VG < VTN): The positive gate pushes holes away from the surface. Immobile, negatively charged ionized acceptors are left behind, forming a depletion region under the oxide (as in the pn junction of Chapter 3).
s4p1.li6: Inversion (VG > VTN): When the gate is positive enough, minority carriers (electrons) are attracted to the surface. The electron density at the surface exceeds the hole density, so the surface is inverted from p-type to n-type. This thin electron layer is the inversion layer, which is exactly the channel of the MOSFET.
s4p1.cv: The MOS capacitance is a nonlinear function of voltage. The total capacitance is modeled as the series combination of the fixed oxide capacitance and a voltage-dependent depletion layer capacitance. In accumulation the capacitance is Cox; in depletion it drops because of the series depletion capacitance; at low frequency in inversion it rises back toward Cox because the electrons gather at the surface again.
s4p1.li7: Adding heavily doped n+ regions on both sides of the MOS capacitor gives an NMOS transistor. It has four terminals: Gate (G), Drain (D), Source (S) and Body (B).
s4p1.li8: The distance between source and drain is the channel length L, and the width of the channel into the page is the channel width W. The current scales with the W/L ratio.
s4p1.li9: Source and drain each form a pn junction with the substrate. These junctions must always stay reverse-biased, otherwise current leaks into the substrate. That is why vSB ≥ 0 in normal operation (the body is usually tied to the lowest voltage).
s4p1.li10: In normal NMOS operation, v<sub>GS</sub>, v<sub>DS</sub> and v<sub>SB</sub> are all positive.
s4p1.li11: VGS ≪ VTN: There is no channel; only a very small leakage current flows.
s4p1.li12: VGS < VTN: The depletion region under the gate merges with the source and drain depletion regions. With no free carriers between them, no current flows between source and drain.
s4p1.li13: VGS > VTN: An electron channel forms between source and drain. If vDS > 0, electrons move from source to drain, so the current iD flows from drain to source.
s4p1.li14: Because the gate is insulated by the oxide and the body junctions are reverse-biased, iG = 0 and iB = 0. This is why the MOSFET has a very high input impedance.

s4fig.mosCap: MOS capacitor (p-type substrate): a negative gate attracts holes to the surface, a small positive gate repels them and leaves ionized acceptors behind, and above V<sub>TN</sub> an inversion layer of electrons forms at the surface.
s4fig.nmos: NMOS transistor: two n<sup>+</sup> regions (source and drain) in a p-type substrate, with the gate on the oxide between them. When V<sub>GS</sub> > V<sub>TN</sub>, an n-type channel forms under the gate and connects source and drain. The channel width W extends into the page.
s4fig.out: NMOS output characteristics (V<sub>TN</sub> = 1 V, K<sub>n</sub> = 1 mA/V<sup>2</sup>). The dashed line is the boundary v<sub>DS</sub> = v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TN</sub>: triode to its left, saturation to its right. In saturation the current is independent of v<sub>DS</sub> and depends only on v<sub>GS</sub>.
s4fig.transfer: Transfer characteristics in saturation (K<sub>n</sub> = 1 mA/V<sup>2</sup>). The enhancement-mode transistor is off at v<sub>GS</sub> = 0; the depletion-mode transistor already conducts at v<sub>GS</sub> = 0 and needs v<sub>GS</sub> < −2 V to turn off.
s4fig.four: Four-resistor biasing: R<sub>1</sub>-R<sub>2</sub> set the gate voltage and R<sub>S</sub> provides negative feedback.
s4fig.two: Two-resistor biasing: no current flows through R<sub>G</sub>, so V<sub>GS</sub> = V<sub>DS</sub> and the transistor is saturated.
s4fig.mirror: NMOS current mirror: M<sub>1</sub> is diode-connected (gate tied to drain), and M<sub>1</sub> and M<sub>2</sub> share the same V<sub>GS</sub>.
s4fig.jfet: n-channel JFET: p<sup>+</sup> gate regions on both sides of an n-type block. The depletion regions of the gate junctions (yellow) extend into the channel and set the channel width W.
s4fig.jfetOut: n-channel JFET output characteristics (I<sub>DSS</sub> = 4 mA, V<sub>P</sub> = −4 V). The dashed line is the boundary v<sub>DS</sub> = v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>P</sub>. The top curve is v<sub>GS</sub> = 0; the JFET does not conduct more than this in normal operation.

s4p2.title: Part 2 · NMOS i-v: Cutoff, Triode and Saturation
s4p2.intro: Depending on v<sub>GS</sub> and v<sub>DS</sub>, the NMOS drain current i<sub>D</sub> follows one of three operating regions. Finding the region is the first step of any circuit analysis, because each region has its own equation.
s4p2.f1: i<sub>D</sub> = K<sub>n</sub>' (W/L) (v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TN</sub> − v<sub>DS</sub>/2) v<sub>DS</sub>     v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TN</sub> ≥ v<sub>DS</sub> ≥ 0
s4p2.li1: Kn' = µnCox'' (A/V2): the process transconductance parameter, the product of electron mobility and oxide capacitance. It depends on the fabrication technology.
s4p2.li2: Kn = Kn'·W/L: the transconductance parameter. The designer controls the W/L ratio; in the same process a wider transistor conducts more current.
s4p2.li3: vGS − VTN is called the overdrive voltage (gate drive). The electron charge in the channel is proportional to it: the more the gate exceeds the threshold, the thicker the channel.
s4p2.ron: For small vDS (vDS/2 ≪ vGS − VTN) the vDS/2 term can be neglected and iD becomes linear in vDS. That is why the output characteristics look like straight lines near the origin. In this region the MOSFET behaves like a resistor between source and drain whose value is set by the gate voltage:
s4p2.ex1: Example: Kn' = 100 µA/V2, VTN = 0.75 V. The W/L required for Ron = 500 Ω: at VGS = 5 V, W/L = 1/[100 µA/V2·(5 − 0.75)·500] = 4.71; at VGS = 3.3 V, W/L = 7.84. With a lower gate voltage, a wider transistor is needed for the same resistance.
s4p2.ex2: Voltage-controlled attenuator: A resistor R and a MOSFET in the triode region form a voltage divider: vO/vS = Ron/(Ron + R) = 1/[1 + R·Kn(VGG − VTN)]. For Kn = 500 µA/V2, VTN = 1 V, R = 2 kΩ and VGG = 1.5 V, vO/vS = 1/(1 + 0.5) = 0.667. To stay in the triode region, vDS ≤ vGS − VTN, so vO ≤ 0.5 V and therefore vS ≤ 0.75 V. The gain is adjusted by VGG.
s4p2.ex3: Voltage-controlled high-pass filter: A series C with the MOSFET in shunt gives T(s) = s/(s + ωo) with cutoff frequency ωo = 1/(RonC) = Kn(VGS − VTN)/C. For Kn = 500 µA/V2, VTN = 1 V, C = 0.02 µF and VGG = 1.5 V, fo = 500 µA/V2·0.5 V / (2π·0.02 µF) = 1.99 kHz. The triode condition requires vS ≤ VGG − VTN = 0.5 V.
s4p2.sat: As vDS increases, the gate-to-channel voltage at the drain end (vGD = vGS − vDS) decreases and the channel becomes thinner near the drain. When vDS = vGS − VTN, vGD = VTN at the drain end and the channel disappears at that point. This is called pinch-off. Beyond it, increasing vDS no longer increases the current; the extra voltage drops across the short depleted region between the pinch-off point and the drain, which electrons cross quickly under the field. The current saturates at a constant value:
s4p2.li4: vDSAT = vGS − VTN: the saturation (pinch-off) voltage. This is the boundary between triode and saturation; substituting vDS = vGS − VTN into the triode equation gives the saturation equation, so the two equations match at the boundary.
s4p2.li5: In saturation the current is controlled only by vGS and grows with its square (square-law). That is why the saturation region is mostly used for analog amplification.
s4p2.li6: The triode region is mostly used in digital circuits (as a switch with a small R<sub>on</sub>) and in voltage-controlled resistor applications.
s4p2.ex4: Example: Kn' = 200 µA/V2, W/L = 5 µm/0.5 µm = 10 (Kn = 2 mA/V2), VDS = 0.25 V. (a) If VGS − VTN < 0: cutoff, ID = 0. (b) VGS − VTN = 0.2 V < VDS: saturation, ID = (2 mA/V2/2)(0.2)2 = 40.0 µA. (c) VGS − VTN = 1.2 V > VDS: triode, ID = 2 mA/V2·(1.2 − 0.125)·0.25 = 538 µA. (d) VGS − VTN = 2.2 V: triode, ID = 1.04 mA.
s4p2.ex5: Example: Kn' = 200 µA/V2, W/L = 10/1, VTN = 0.75 V and VGS = 2 V (overdrive 1.25 V). (a) VDS = 0.2 V < 1.25 V: triode, ID = 2 mA/V2·(1.25 − 0.1)·0.2 = 460 µA. (b) VDS = 2.5 V > 1.25 V: saturation, ID = (2 mA/V2/2)(1.25)2 = 1.56 mA. (c) If VGS < VTN: cutoff and ID = 0. With Kn' = 300 µA/V2 the currents would be 1.5 times larger (690 µA and 2.34 mA).
s4p2.gm: Transconductance describes how much a small change in gate voltage changes the drain current (unit A/V or S). It directly sets the gain of an amplifier, so it is one of the most important parameters in analog design. Differentiating the saturation equation:
s4p2.ex6: Extracting parameters from a graph: Two measurements in saturation: 395 µA at VGS = 4 V and 140 µA at VGS = 3 V. Taking the ratio of the two equations gives (4 − VTN)2/(3 − VTN)2 = 395/140, which yields VTN ≈ 1.5 V and Kn = 125 µA/V2. Since VTN > 0, this is an enhancement-mode transistor.
s4p2.clm: In reality the saturation current is not perfectly constant. As v<sub>DS</sub> rises above v<sub>DSAT</sub>, the pinch-off point moves toward the source: the depleted length ΔL increases and the effective channel length L − ΔL decreases. A shorter channel gives a slightly larger current. This is modeled by adding a correction factor to the saturation equation:
s4p2.lambda: λ: the channel-length modulation parameter, typically between 0.001 V-1 and 0.1 V-1. The smaller λ, the flatter the curves in saturation and the better the transistor works as a current source. In short-channel transistors ΔL matters more, so λ is larger.

s4p3.title: Part 3 · Depletion-Mode MOSFET and Body Effect
s4p3.intro: In the NMOS considered so far, VTN > 0: there is no channel at vGS = 0, and the gate has to create one. Such transistors are called enhancement-mode devices. A device whose channel exists from the start is called a depletion-mode device.
s4p3.li2: During fabrication, an n-type channel is built in under the gate by ion implantation. This built-in channel connects source and drain through a resistive path from the start.
s4p3.li3: Therefore drain current flows even at vGS = 0. To turn the transistor off, a negative gate voltage must push the electrons out of the channel, that is, deplete it. This is where the name comes from.
s4p3.li4: The i-v equations are the same as for the enhancement-mode device; VTN is simply negative. A positive vGS attracts even more electrons into the channel and the current increases further.
s4p3.transfer: The transfer characteristic is the plot of iD versus vGS for a fixed vDS (in the output characteristic the x-axis was vDS; here it is vGS). In saturation it is a parabola starting at VTN. Where the curve meets the x-axis gives VTN, and its sign tells the transistor type directly.
s4p3.ex1: Example: Depletion-mode NMOS, VTN = −3 V, Kn = 250 µA/V2, VGS = 0 and VDS = 6 V. Since VGS − VTN = 3 V ≤ VDS, it is in saturation: ID = (250 µA/V2/2)(0 + 3)2 = 1.13 mA. With λ = 0.025 V-1, ID = 1.13 mA·(1 + 0.025·6) = 1.29 mA.
s4p3.ex2: Example: A depletion-mode NMOS (VTN = −2 V, Kn' = 100 µA/V2, W/L = 10/1) has its gate tied to the source (VGS = 0) and its drain connected to +10 V through 100 kΩ. In saturation ID would be (1 mA/V2/2)(2)2 = 2 mA, but that would require a 200 V drop across 100 kΩ, which a 10 V supply cannot provide. So the transistor is in the triode region: (10 − VDS)/105 = 10-3(2 − VDS/2)VDS. Solving the quadratic gives VDS = 0.0504 V and ID = 99.5 µA. Nearly all the voltage drops across the resistor, and the transistor behaves like a small resistance.
s4p3.body: So far we assumed source and body are at the same voltage (vSB = 0). If the body is more negative than the source (vSB > 0), the source-body junction is reverse-biased more strongly and the depletion region under the gate widens. With more negative charge in the depletion region, forming the inversion layer becomes harder, so the threshold voltage increases:
s4p3.li6: γ: the body-effect parameter (√V). It depends on the substrate doping and oxide thickness, that is, on the fabrication process.
s4p3.li7: 2φF: the surface potential parameter (V), typically around 0.6 V.
s4p3.li8: In integrated circuits the bodies are usually shared and tied to the lowest voltage, so every transistor whose source is above ground experiences the body effect. It must not be forgotten in the analysis.
s4p3.ex3: Example: VTO = 1 V, γ = 0.7 √V, 2φF = 0.6 V, VSB = 3 V, Kn' = 100 µA/V2, W/L = 8/1 and VGS = 2.5 V. VTN = 1 + 0.7(√3.6 − √0.6) = 1.79 V. (a) VDS = 5 V > VGS − VTN = 0.71 V: saturation, ID = (800 µA/V2/2)(0.71)2 = 202 µA. (b) VDS = 0.5 V < 0.71 V: triode, ID = 800 µA/V2·(0.71 − 0.25)·0.5 = 184 µA. Without the body effect (VTN = 1 V) the current would be much larger for the same VGS.

s4p4.title: Part 4 · PMOS Transistor and MOSFET Symbols
s4p4.intro: A PMOS transistor is the NMOS with all n and p regions swapped: p+ source and drain in an n-type substrate. The channel is formed by holes. The logic is the same as for NMOS; only the signs of the voltages and the current are reversed.
s4p4.li1: Forming a p-type inversion layer under the gate requires attracting holes to the surface, which means vGS < 0.
s4p4.li2: The threshold voltage VTP is negative. For current to flow, vGS ≤ VTP, that is, the gate must be more negative than VTP relative to the source.
s4p4.li3: To keep the source-substrate and drain-substrate junctions reverse-biased, vSB ≤ 0 and vDB ≤ 0 (the body is usually tied to the highest voltage).
s4p4.li4: In a PMOS the current flows from source to drain. Defining iD as the current flowing out of the drain, the equations give a positive current.
s4p4.li5: Hole mobility is about 2–3 times lower than electron mobility, so K<sub>p</sub>' = µ<sub>p</sub>C<sub>ox</sub>'' is also smaller. To conduct the same current, a PMOS is usually made wider (larger W/L) than an NMOS.
s4p4.f2: Triode: i<sub>D</sub> = K<sub>p</sub>'(W/L)(v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TP</sub> − v<sub>DS</sub>/2)v<sub>DS</sub>     0 ≤ |v<sub>DS</sub>| ≤ |v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TP</sub>|
s4p4.signs: In the triode equation both (v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TP</sub> − v<sub>DS</sub>/2) and v<sub>DS</sub> are negative, so their product is positive. To avoid sign bookkeeping, PMOS can be written with v<sub>SG</sub>, v<sub>SD</sub> and |V<sub>TP</sub>|: the equations then become identical to those of the NMOS.
s4p4.f4: PMOS body effect: V<sub>TP</sub> = V<sub>TO</sub> − γ(√(v<sub>BS</sub> + 2φ<sub>F</sub>) − √(2φ<sub>F</sub>))
s4p4.bodyP: In a PMOS, when the body is more positive than the source (v<sub>BS</sub> > 0), V<sub>TP</sub> becomes more negative: |V<sub>TP</sub>| grows and the transistor becomes harder to turn on.
s4p4.ex1: Example: Kp' = 40 µA/V2, W/L = 20/1, VTP = −0.75 V, VDS = −0.2 V. (a) VGS = −1.1 V: VGS − VTP = −0.35 V and |VDS| = 0.2 V < 0.35 V, triode. ID = 40 µA/V2·20·(−0.35 + 0.1)(−0.2) = 40.0 µA. (b) VGS = −1.3 V: triode, ID = 72.0 µA. (c) If the body effect makes VTP = −0.995 V, then at VGS = −1.1 V, VGS − VTP = −0.105 V and |VDS| = 0.2 V > 0.105 V: saturation, ID = (800 µA/V2/2)(0.105)2 = 4.41 µA. Even a small threshold shift can reduce the current by a factor of ten.
s4p4.li6: A broken channel line means enhancement mode (no channel at vGS = 0); a solid line means depletion mode (the channel exists from the start).
s4p4.li7: The arrow on the body terminal shows the direction of the body-channel pn junction: from the p body into the n channel for NMOS, that is, inward; outward for PMOS.
s4p4.li8: If the body is tied to the source or is not important in the circuit, the 3-terminal symbol is used; the arrow marks the source and shows the current direction. These simplified symbols are the most common in VLSI logic design.
s4p4.li9: The MOSFET is a symmetric device: source and drain are physically identical, and the circuit voltages decide which is which. In an NMOS the n+ region at the higher voltage is the drain; in a PMOS the p+ region at the lower voltage is the drain.

s4p5.title: Part 5 · Layout, Capacitances and SPICE Model
s4p5.h1: Two parameters that define a process
s4p5.li1: Minimum feature size F: the width of the smallest line or space that can be reliably transferred to the wafer surface with a given generation of lithography tools.
s4p5.li2: Alignment tolerance T: the maximum misalignment that can occur between two mask levels.
s4p5.li3: Layout ground rules are usually written in terms of a single Λ: F = 2Λ and T = F/2 = Λ. Depending on the technology, Λ can be 1, 0.5, 0.25 µm, etc. This lets the same layout be scaled to different technologies.
s4p5.h2: Mask sequence for a polysilicon-gate transistor
s4p5.st1: Mask 1: defines the active area (thin-oxide region) of the transistor.
s4p5.st2: Mask 2: defines the polysilicon gate; aligned to Mask 1.
s4p5.st3: Mask 3: marks the contact windows; aligned to Mask 2.
s4p5.st4: Mask 4: delineates the metal pattern; aligned to Mask 3.
s4p5.selfAlign: The transistor channel is formed where the first two masks intersect. Source and drain are formed wherever the active area is not covered by the gate: during the n+ implantation the gate acts as a mask, so source and drain are automatically aligned to the gate (self-aligned). Recall the IC fabrication steps from Chapter 2.
s4p5.capWhy: Capacitances inside electronic devices limit their high-frequency performance: they set the switching speed of logic circuits and the frequency up to which amplifiers provide useful gain. MOSFET capacitances depend on the operating region and are nonlinear functions of the terminal voltages.
s4p5.li5: CGSO, CGDO (F/m): the overlap capacitances per unit width, from the part of the gate that extends over the source and drain.
s4p5.li6: CSB, CDB: the depletion capacitances of the source-bulk and drain-bulk pn junctions: CSB = CJAS + CJSWPS, CDB = CJAD + CJSWPD. A is the junction bottom area, P its perimeter, CJ (F/m2) the bottom and CJSW (F/m) the sidewall capacitance.
s4p5.li7: Triode: the channel is connected to both source and drain, and CGC is split equally between them.
s4p5.li8: Saturation: the channel is pinched off at the drain end, so the drain is no longer connected to the channel. Two-thirds of CGC goes to the source, and only the overlap remains in CGD.
s4p5.li9: Cutoff: the conducting channel is completely gone. The gate sees source and drain only through the overlaps, and a gate-bulk capacitance CGB appears.
s4p5.ex1: Example: Cox'' = 1.4 fF/µm2, CGSO = CGDO = 4 fF/µm, W = 10 µm, L = 1 µm. CGC = 1.4·10·1 = 14 fF, overlap = 4·10 = 40 fF. (a) Triode: CGS = CGD = 7 + 40 = 47 fF. (b) Saturation: CGS = (2/3)·14 + 40 = 49 fF, CGD = 40 fF. (c) Cutoff: CGS = CGD = 40 fF. At these dimensions the overlap capacitances dominate.

s4p6.title: Part 6 · MOSFET Biasing and Current Mirror
s4p6.intro: Before a transistor can be used as an amplifier or a switch, its DC operating point, the Q-point = (ID, VDS), must be set. This is called biasing. The approach is the same as the diode analysis of Chapter 3: guess a region, solve, check.
s4p6.st2: Use circuit analysis to find V<sub>GS</sub> (remember that I<sub>G</sub> = I<sub>B</sub> = 0).
s4p6.st3: Use V<sub>GS</sub> to calculate I<sub>D</sub>, and I<sub>D</sub> to find V<sub>DS</sub>.
s4p6.st4: Check the assumption: for saturation, VDS ≥ VGS − VTN must hold.
s4p6.st5: If it does not hold, assume the other region and solve again.
s4p6.note: Note: an enhancement-mode transistor with VDS = VGS (gate tied to drain) is always in saturation, because VDS = VGS > VGS − VTN.
s4p6.li1: Provides excellent bias for discrete circuits. A single supply provides both the gate bias and the drain current.
s4p6.li2: RS provides negative feedback: if ID increases, the voltage across RS rises, VGS drops and ID decreases again. This keeps the Q-point stable against variations in device parameters and temperature.
s4p6.li3: For the analysis, the gate network is first replaced by its Thévenin equivalent: V<sub>EQ</sub> = V<sub>DD</sub>R<sub>2</sub>/(R<sub>1</sub> + R<sub>2</sub>), R<sub>EQ</sub> = R<sub>1</sub>||R<sub>2</sub>. Since I<sub>G</sub> = 0, there is no voltage drop across R<sub>EQ</sub>.
s4p6.li4: Two-resistor biasing uses fewer components. Both are generally used to bias the transistor in saturation.
s4p6.ex1: Example 1 (four-resistor): VDD = 10 V, VEQ = 4 V, REQ = 600 kΩ, RD = 75 kΩ, RS = 39 kΩ, Kn = 25 µA/V2, VTN = 1 V. Assume saturation. Gate loop: VEQ = VGS + IDRS = VGS + (KnRS/2)(VGS − VTN)2. Substituting gives VGS2 + 0.05VGS − 7.21 = 0 with roots 2.66 V and −2.71 V. Since −2.71 V < VTN, that root means cutoff and is discarded. VGS = 2.66 V, ID = 12.5 µA/V2·(1.66)2 = 34.4 µA, VDS = 10 − 34.4 µA·114 kΩ = 6.08 V. Check: 6.08 V > 1.66 V, saturation confirmed. Q-point = (34.4 µA, 6.08 V).
s4p6.ex2: Example 2 (with body effect): In the same type of circuit, VEQ = 6 V, RS = 22 kΩ, RD + RS = 40 kΩ, VTN = 1 + 0.5(√(VSB + 0.6) − √0.6) and VSB = IDRS. Now VGS and VTN both depend on ID, so there is no closed-form solution. Iterate: estimate ID, find VGS = 6 − 22000ID and VSB = 22000ID, compute VTN, find the new ID, and repeat until it matches the estimate (easy with Excel). The result is ID = 88.0 µA, VDS = 10 − 40000ID = 6.48 V > VGS − VTN, so saturation is confirmed. Q-point = (88.0 µA, 6.48 V).
s4p6.ex3: Example 3 (two-resistor): VDD = 3.3 V, RD = 10 kΩ, Kn = 260 µA/V2, VTN = 1 V. Since VGS = VDS, it is saturated. VGS = VDD − IDRD = 3.3 − 1.3(VGS − 1)2. The roots are 2.00 V and −0.769 V; the negative root means cutoff and is discarded. VGS = VDS = 2.00 V and ID = 130 µA. Q-point = (130 µA, 2.00 V).
s4p6.ex4: Example 4 (biasing in the triode region): Gate tied directly to VDD = 4 V, RD = 1.6 kΩ, Kn = 250 µA/V2, VTN = 1 V. Assuming saturation gives ID = 125 µA/V2·(3)2 = 1.13 mA and VDS = 4 − 1600·1.13 mA = 2.2 V. But 2.2 V < VGS − VTN = 3 V, so the assumption is wrong. Redo with the triode equation: 4 − VDS = 1600·250 µA/V2·(3 − VDS/2)VDS, i.e. VDS2 − 11VDS + 20 = 0. The roots are 8.7 V (larger than VDD, impossible) and 2.3 V. ID = (4 − 2.3)/1.6 kΩ = 1.06 mA. Q-point = (1.06 mA, 2.3 V).
s4p6.ex5: Example 5 (PMOS, two-resistor): Source at +15 V, gate tied to drain, drain to ground through 220 kΩ. Kp = 50 µA/V2, VTP = −2 V. Since VDS = VGS, it is saturated. Loop: 15 + VGS − 220 kΩ·(25 µA/V2)(VGS + 2)2 = 0. The roots are −0.369 V and −3.45 V. At −0.369 V > VTP the transistor would be off, so VGS = −3.45 V. ID = 25 µA/V2·(−1.45)2 = 52.5 µA. Q-point = (52.5 µA, −3.45 V).
s4p6.cs: An ideal current source delivers a fixed current regardless of the voltage across it. Since the current of a saturated MOSFET is nearly independent of vDS (for small λ), it behaves like a good current source. However, the current varies with (VGS − VTN)2, so setting VGS with a fixed voltage is unreliable: small variations in VTN and Kn change the current a lot. The solution is the current mirror.
s4p6.mirror: I<sub>REF</sub> is forced through M<sub>1</sub>. Being diode-connected, M<sub>1</sub> is automatically saturated and sets the V<sub>GS</sub> needed to carry I<sub>REF</sub>. M<sub>2</sub> shares gate and source with M<sub>1</sub>, so it sees the same V<sub>GS</sub>. If both are identical (same V<sub>TN</sub>, K<sub>n</sub>', λ and W/L) and saturated:
s4p6.f1: I<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>REF</sub> · (1 + λV<sub>DS2</sub>) / (1 + λV<sub>DS1</sub>)     V<sub>DS1</sub> = V<sub>DS2</sub> ise I<sub>O</sub> = I<sub>REF</sub>
s4p6.ratio: If the transistors are not identical, the output current scales with the W/L ratios. This makes it possible to derive currents of any ratio from a single reference (for example, (W/L)<sub>2</sub> = 5(W/L)<sub>1</sub> gives I<sub>O</sub> ≈ 5I<sub>REF</sub>):
s4p6.ro: Because of channel-length modulation, the output current changes slightly with vO. How close the source is to ideal is measured by its output resistance (infinite for an ideal source):
s4p6.ex1m: Example: IREF = 50 µA, VO = 12 V, VTN = 1 V, Kn = 150 µA/V2, λ = 0.0133 V-1. For M1, VDS1 = VGS1 = VTN + √(2IREF/[Kn(1 + λVDS1)]); by trial and error VDS1 = 1.81 V. IO = 50 µA·(1 + 0.0133·12)/(1 + 0.0133·1.81) = 56.6 µA. Check that M2 is saturated: VDS2 = 12 V > VGS2 − VTN = 0.81 V, it holds. Ro = (1 + 0.0133·12)/(0.0133·56.6 µA) = 1.54 MΩ. IO differs from IREF by 13% because the VDS values of the two transistors differ.
s4p6.h5: The resistor problem in integrated circuits
s4p6.res: A resistor R is needed to set I<sub>REF</sub>, but in a fully integrated circuit the resistor is built on chip as R = ρL/(tW) and takes a lot of area. For example, a 95 kΩ resistor with W = 1 µm needs L = 9500 µm, an area of 9500 µm<sup>2</sup>, while a typical NMOS occupies 3–4 µm<sup>2</sup>. The solution is to replace R with a saturated MOSFET. In the example design, a PMOS (M<sub>6</sub>) with W/L = 1/13.6 replaces a 274 kΩ resistor and provides the same 25 µA. Several mirrors derive different currents (such as 50 µA, 125 µA, 25 µA) from a single reference through the choice of W/L ratios.

s4p7.title: Part 7 · Junction Field-Effect Transistor (JFET)
s4p7.intro: In a JFET there is no oxide between gate and channel; the channel is controlled by the depletion regions of reverse-biased pn junctions. Since the gate junction is kept reverse-biased, the gate current is very small: the JFET has a much lower input current and a much higher input impedance than the BJT.
s4p7.li1: In an n-channel JFET, the channel region is an n-type semiconductor block. Current enters the channel at the drain and exits at the source.
s4p7.li2: The gate is formed by two p+n junctions (the two p+ regions are connected together).
s4p7.li3: Since the channel exists from the start, the JFET is inherently a depletion-mode device: it conducts at vGS = 0 and the gate can only narrow the channel.
s4p7.li4: In the triode region the JFET is also a voltage-controlled resistor. The channel resistance follows from the geometry:
s4p7.f1: R<sub>CH</sub> = ρL / (tW)     ρ: channel resistivity, L: channel length, W: channel width between the depletion regions, t: channel depth
s4p7.li5: vGS = 0: the gate junctions form only a small depletion region from their built-in potential. The channel is at its widest, and the gate is isolated from the channel.
s4p7.li6: VP < vGS < 0: the gate-source junction is reverse-biased. The depletion regions grow into the channel, the width becomes W' < W and the channel resistance increases. With the junction reverse-biased, iG ≈ 0.
s4p7.li7: vGS = VP < 0: the depletion regions from both sides meet in the middle and the channel closes completely (pinch-off). The channel resistance becomes infinite and no current flows. VP is the pinch-off voltage; it is negative for an n-channel JFET and plays the role of VTN in the MOSFET.
s4p7.h3: Pinch-off at the drain end with v<sub>DS</sub>
s4p7.li8: With v<sub>GS</sub> fixed, increasing v<sub>DS</sub> raises the voltage along the channel from source to drain. The reverse bias of the gate junction is largest at the drain end (v<sub>DG</sub> = v<sub>DS</sub> − v<sub>GS</sub>), so the depletion region is wider near the drain and the channel becomes wedge-shaped.
s4p7.li9: When vDS = vDSP = vGS − VP, the channel closes completely at the drain end. Beyond this point iD saturates (the same idea as pinch-off in the MOSFET).
s4p7.li10: At larger vDS, the JFET also exhibits channel-length modulation, as the MOSFET does.
s4p7.li11: In all regions, iG ≈ 0 for vGS ≤ 0. If vGS becomes positive, the gate junction is forward-biased and the gate starts drawing current; the JFET is not operated this way.
s4p7.li12: IDSS: the saturation current at vGS = 0 (drain-source current with the gate shorted). It is the largest normal current of the JFET. Typical values: −25 V < VP < 0 and 10 µA < IDSS < 10 A.
s4p7.li13: The equations have exactly the same form as for the depletion-mode MOSFET: replace VTN with VP and Kn with 2IDSS/VP2. That is, IDSS = (Kn/2)VP2.
s4p7.pjfet: Reversing the n and p regions of the n-channel JFET gives the p-channel JFET. The direction of the channel current and the polarities of all bias voltages are reversed: VP > 0, and a positive vGS is needed to turn it off.
s4p7.symNote: The arrow on the gate shows the direction of the gate-channel pn junction: into the channel for an n-JFET, outward for a p-JFET. Like MOSFETs, JFETs are symmetric, and the circuit voltages determine source and drain.
s4p7.jcap: The JFET capacitances C<sub>GS</sub> and C<sub>GD</sub> are the depletion-layer capacitances of the reverse-biased pn junctions forming the gate, so they depend on bias. SPICE defaults: V<sub>P</sub> (VTO) = −2 V, BETA = I<sub>DSS</sub>/V<sub>P</sub><sup>2</sup> = 100 µA/V<sup>2</sup>, λ = C<sub>GS</sub> = C<sub>GD</sub> = 0.
s4p7.h7: Biasing a JFET and a depletion-mode MOSFET
s4p7.bias: Since depletion-mode devices conduct at vGS = 0, it is enough to ground the gate and place a resistor RS at the source (self-bias): the current drops a voltage across RS, which raises the source and reverse-biases the gate-source junction automatically. Assumptions: the JFET is pinched off, the gate junction is reverse-biased and IG = 0.
s4p7.ex1: Example: n-channel JFET, IDSS = 5 mA, VP = −5 V, RS = 1 kΩ, RD = 2 kΩ, VDD = 12 V, gate grounded. Since IS = ID, VGS = −IDRS = −IDSSRS(1 − VGS/VP)2 = −5(1 + VGS/5)2. The roots are −1.91 V and −13.1 V. At −13.1 V < VP the JFET would be cut off, so that root is discarded. VGS = −1.91 V, ID = 1.91 mA, VDS = 12 − 1.91 mA·3 kΩ = 6.27 V. Check: VDS = 6.27 V > VGS − VP = 3.09 V, pinch-off confirmed; the gate-source junction is reverse-biased by 1.91 V. Q-point = (1.91 mA, 6.27 V). A depletion-mode NMOS with VTN = −5 V and Kn = 2IDSS/VP2 = 0.4 mA/V2 gives the same result in this circuit.

fetSim.vsbHint: Body effect: reverse-bias the body relative to the source and the threshold shifts.
fetSim.outHint: The pink curve is the selected v<sub>GS</sub> and the dot is the operating point. Gray curves are other v<sub>GS</sub> values; the dashed line is the triode/saturation boundary.
fetSim.trHint: i<sub>D</sub>(v<sub>GS</sub>) for the selected v<sub>DS</sub>. The dashed vertical line is the threshold voltage.
fetSim.note: The simulation uses K<sub>n</sub>' = 100 µA/V<sup>2</sup>, W/L = 10 for NMOS and K<sub>p</sub>' = 40 µA/V<sup>2</sup>, W/L = 25 for PMOS (the PMOS is wider because of the lower hole mobility, so both types have K = 1 mA/V<sup>2</sup>). V<sub>TO</sub> = ±1 V (enhancement), ∓2 V (depletion), γ = 0.5 √V, 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.6 V, λ = 0.05 V<sup>-1</sup>. The PMOS plots use −v<sub>DS</sub> and −v<sub>GS</sub> on their axes. The drawing is not to scale.
fetSim.tryHint: In each one, watch the cross-section, the explanation on the right and the dot on both plots together.
fetSim.t1: In NMOS enhancement with v<sub>DS</sub> = 1 V, move v<sub>GS</sub> from −2 V to 4 V. First holes accumulate at the surface, then a depletion region forms, and once V<sub>TN</sub> = 1 V is exceeded an electron channel appears.
fetSim.t2: At v<sub>GS</sub> = 3 V, increase v<sub>DS</sub> from 0 to 6 V. The channel thins at the drain end and vanishes there at v<sub>DS</sub> = v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>TN</sub> = 2 V. After that the current stays constant. Turn on λ and repeat.
fetSim.t3: Switch to depletion and set v<sub>GS</sub> = 0: the channel already exists and current flows. To turn the transistor off, bring v<sub>GS</sub> below −2 V. Notice how the transfer characteristic has shifted to the left.
fetSim.t4: Switch to PMOS: all voltages are negative and the channel is formed by holes, but the behavior is the same. Then increase the body bias: the threshold shifts and the current drops for the same v<sub>GS</sub>.

jfetSim.warn: The gate junction is forward-biased: the gate starts drawing current (i<sub>G</sub> ≠ 0). A JFET is not normally operated this way; the gate junction is always kept reverse-biased.
jfetSim.outHint: The pink curve is the selected v<sub>GS</sub>; gray curves are v<sub>GS</sub> = 0, −1, −2, −3 V. The dashed line is the boundary v<sub>DS</sub> = v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>P</sub>.
jfetSim.trHint: i<sub>D</sub>(v<sub>GS</sub>) for the selected v<sub>DS</sub>. The curve drops to zero at V<sub>P</sub> and reaches I<sub>DSS</sub> at v<sub>GS</sub> = 0 (in pinch-off).
jfetSim.note: The simulation uses I<sub>DSS</sub> = 4 mA, V<sub>P</sub> = −4 V (+4 V for p-channel), a gate junction built-in potential of 0.8 V and λ = 0.03 V<sup>-1</sup>. The p-channel plots use −v<sub>DS</sub> and −v<sub>GS</sub> on their axes. The drawing is not to scale.
jfetSim.tryHint: Watch the shape of the depletion regions together with the dot on both plots.
jfetSim.t1: With v<sub>DS</sub> = 0.5 V, lower v<sub>GS</sub> from 0 to −4 V. The depletion regions grow from both sides and narrow the channel, and at V<sub>P</sub> = −4 V they meet in the middle and close it.
jfetSim.t2: At v<sub>GS</sub> = −1 V, increase v<sub>DS</sub>. The reverse bias is larger at the drain end, so the channel narrows more there. At v<sub>DS</sub> = v<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>P</sub> = 3 V the drain end pinches off.
jfetSim.t3: Set v<sub>GS</sub> = 0 and v<sub>DS</sub> = 6 V. The current is I<sub>DSS</sub> = 4 mA, the largest current the JFET delivers in normal operation. Notice that the transfer characteristic is a parabola from V<sub>P</sub> to I<sub>DSS</sub>.
jfetSim.t4: Raise v<sub>GS</sub> above 0: the depletion regions shrink, but the gate junction becomes forward-biased and the gate draws current. Then switch to p-channel: all signs are reversed.
